Random forests

Source: R/random_forest.r
random_forest.Rd

Grows a random forest (Breiman 2001) of classification or regression trees on a feature table: to predict each sample's class (disease or health, body site) or a number (age, a clinical score), to rank the features by importance, and to estimate how well that works, by cross-validation and out of bag. The trees are an exact port of scikit-learn's, and the workflow is q2-sample-classifier's.

Usage

random_forest(
  counts,
  y,
  data = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  norm = "percent",
  pseudocount = NULL,
  n_trees = 500L,
  max_features = NULL,
  min_samples_leaf = 1L,
  min_samples_split = 2L,
  max_depth = NULL,
  criterion = NULL,
  class_weight = NULL,
  max_samples = NULL,
  importance = "impurity",
  n_folds = 5L,
  folds = NULL,
  keep_forest = TRUE,
  seed = 0L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of feature values (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the table types listed under "Input Types" (sparse tables stay sparse). Typically counts.

y

What to predict: a vector with one value per sample, or the name of a column of data. A factor, character or logical y makes a classification forest (the classes are its values, or a factor's levels); a numeric y, a regression forest. Samples whose y is NA are left out, with a warning.

data

A data frame of sample metadata, with one row per sample (matched to counts by row names when both have them), when y names one of its columns. Default: NULL

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

norm

How to normalize each sample before growing the trees: 'percent' (relative abundances, the default), 'none' (the values as given, for any numeric table), or one of normalize()'s other choices. Trees don't change under monotone transforms of a feature, so only transforms across features (percent, clr, chord, ...) matter. Default: 'percent'

pseudocount

Value added to counts to handle zeros when norm = 'clr' or 'log'. Ignored for other normalization methods. See Pseudocount section.

n_trees

The number of trees in each forest. Default: 500

max_features

How many features each split chooses among: a count, a fraction of the features (below 1), 'sqrt', 'log2', or 'all'; NULL for scikit-learn's defaults ('sqrt' for classification, 'all' for regression). A vector of these makes a grid (see Details). Default: NULL

min_samples_leaf

The fewest (distinct) samples a leaf may hold. A vector of values makes a grid (see Details). Default: 1

min_samples_split

The fewest (distinct) samples a node needs to be split; at least twice min_samples_leaf is used. Default: 2

max_depth

The deepest a tree may grow, or NULL for no limit. Default: NULL

criterion

The impurity to split on: 'gini' (the default for classification) or 'entropy'; 'squared_error' for regression. Default: NULL

class_weight

Weights for the classes (classification only): NULL (equal), 'balanced' (\(n / (k n_c)\) for a class of \(n_c\) of the \(n\) training samples, \(k\) classes), 'balanced_subsample' (the same, computed on each tree's bootstrap sample), or a named numeric vector of weights (classes not named get 1). As in scikit-learn 1.9, weights other than 'balanced_subsample' drive a weighted bootstrap (samples are drawn in proportion to their class weight). Default: NULL

max_samples

The size of each tree's bootstrap sample: NULL (as many draws as training samples), a count, or a fraction (below 1) of the training samples (of their total class weight, with class_weight). Default: NULL

importance

Which feature importances to compute: 'impurity' (mean decrease in impurity, free), 'permutation' (out-of-bag permutation importance), or 'both'. Default: 'impurity'

n_folds

The number of cross-validation folds; 0 or 1 for none (out-of-bag estimates only). Default: 5

folds

A fold for each sample instead (any labels; each label is a fold), which overrides n_folds and seed for the folds. Matched to the samples like y. Default: NULL

keep_forest

Keep the full-data forest in the result, for predict(). Default: TRUE

seed

An integer seed for the bootstraps, the trees' feature draws, the folds and the permutations. The same seed gives the same forest for any cpus. Default: 0

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), is the CPU cores this R process may use, within any limits set on it. Results are the same for any cpus.

Value

A list of class ecodive_random_forest:

importance

A data frame, one row per feature, sorted by the requested importance (largest first): feature, impurity (the full-data forest's), impurity_cv_mean and impurity_cv_sd (over the cross-validation folds' forests; q2 reports the mean), and, with importance = 'permutation' or 'both', permutation and permutation_sd.

predictions

A data frame, one row per sample: sample, observed, predicted (cross-validated: by the forest of the fold that held the sample out), fold, oob_predicted, and for classification one cross-validated probability per class (prob_<class>).

performance

A named numeric vector. Classification: accuracy (cross-validated), accuracy_fold_mean, accuracy_fold_sd (over folds, sd with divisor n, as q2), balanced_accuracy, baseline_accuracy (the largest class's share), accuracy_ratio, auc (two classes) or auc_macro and auc_micro, and oob_accuracy. Regression: mse, r_squared, mse_fold_mean, mse_fold_sd, slope, intercept and r (of the predicted on the observed values, as q2), and oob_r_squared. Without cross-validation, only the OOB values are not NA.

confusion

Classification: the observed (rows) by predicted (columns) counts, cross-validated (out of bag without cross-validation).

roc

Classification: a data frame class, fpr, tpr, threshold: scikit-learn's roc_curve() of each class against the rest (only the second class with two classes), and for more than two classes q2's 'micro' and 'macro' averages; from the cross-validated probabilities (out of bag without cross-validation).

tuning

With a grid: a data frame of training_set ('full' or 'fold <k>'), max_features, min_samples_leaf, oob_error and chosen.

forest

With keep_forest: the full-data forest, for predict().

Attributes: method ('random_forest'), type ('classification' or 'regression'), n_trees, max_features and min_samples_leaf (of the full-data forest: as chosen, with a grid), criterion, class_weight and n_folds.

Details

The trees

Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample of the training samples (drawn with replacement; the number of draws of each sample is its weight), splitting each node at the threshold, over a random subset of max_features features, that most reduces the weighted impurity: Gini or entropy for classes, the squared error for numbers. Trees grow until their leaves are pure or reach min_samples_leaf, min_samples_split or max_depth. A tree predicts the (weighted) class fractions or mean of the leaf a sample falls in, and the forest averages its trees: class probabilities (soft voting, as scikit-learn), whose largest gives the predicted class (the first class on ties), or the mean of the trees' predictions.

This is scikit-learn 1.9.1's RandomForestClassifier and RandomForestRegressor, ported to C: given the same random draws, the trees are identical (the tests check every node against scikit-learn's). The draws themselves come from ecodive's PCG generator, one stream per tree, so a forest is the same on any number of threads, and differs from scikit-learn's as a different seed would.

Out of bag and cross-validated

About a third of the samples are left out of each tree's bootstrap. Predicting each sample from only the trees that never saw it gives out-of-bag (OOB) predictions and accuracy (or \(R^2\)) for free. Cross-validation grows a separate forest on each fold's training samples and predicts its held-out samples (q2-sample-classifier's classify-samples-ncv and regress-samples-ncv): with n_folds folds, stratified by class for classification (as scikit-learn's StratifiedKFold), or plain (KFold) for regression. Both are honest estimates of how well the forest predicts new samples; cross-validation also gives ROC curves, a confusion matrix and fold-to-fold variation. A full-data forest is also grown: it gives the OOB results, the reported importances and predict().

Choosing settings

A vector of max_features or min_samples_leaf values makes a grid (all their combinations). Within each training set (each fold's, and the full data), a forest is grown for every grid point and the one with the lowest out-of-bag error is kept (the first on ties). The held-out samples never choose a setting, so the cross-validated estimates stay honest. The tuning element lists every grid point's OOB error.

Importance

'impurity' importance (mean decrease in impurity, scikit-learn's feature_importances_) is each feature's share of the trees' total impurity decrease, averaged over trees and scaled to sum to 1. It is biased toward features with many distinct values (Strobl et al. 2007). 'permutation' importance (Breiman 2001) permutes each feature among each tree's out-of-bag samples and records how much the tree's out-of-bag error (misclassification rate, or mean squared error) grows; it is the mean over all trees (a tree that doesn't split on the feature adds 0), with its standard deviation over trees. Importances measure association with the prediction, not effects; correlated features share it.

Features should not be filtered by their association with y before cross-validation: that leaks the held-out samples into the model and inflates the estimates. Relative abundances are compositional, so a feature's importance can reflect changes in others; see "Machine learning" below on transforms (Yerke et al. 2024 found relative abundances did best with random forests).

Recipes

  • q2-sample-classifier's settings: n_trees = 100, n_folds = 5, norm = 'none' (q2 passes the table it's given).

  • randomForest's scaled permutation importance (its default importance(fit)): importance = 'permutation', then permutation / (permutation_sd / sqrt(n_trees)).

  • A microbiota maturity index (Subramanian et al. 2014): a regression forest of age on healthy children's samples, then predict() for the others; their relative maturity is the predicted minus a spline of predicted age on age in the healthy children.

Differences from scikit-learn, q2-sample-classifier, randomForest and ranger

  • Random draws: PCG streams, not numpy's MT19937, so forests differ from scikit-learn's as with a different random_state. (A parity mode that reproduces scikit-learn's draws is used by the tests.)

  • Defaults: 500 trees (randomForest's and ranger's; scikit-learn's and q2's 100), with scikit-learn's max_features (all features for regression, where randomForest uses a third) and leaf sizes (1 for regression, where randomForest and ranger use 5). Tables are relative abundances by default (norm = 'percent').

  • Soft voting: classes are predicted from the mean of the trees' class probabilities, as scikit-learn; randomForest counts votes.

  • Importances: impurity importances sum to 1, as scikit-learn's; randomForest's MeanDecreaseGini and ranger's 'impurity' are not scaled. Permutation importance is unscaled (randomForest's scale = FALSE, ranger's).

  • Never out of bag: a sample that every bootstrap drew gets NA as its OOB prediction, with a warning, and is left out of the OOB scores; scikit-learn predicts 0 for it.

  • Folds: as scikit-learn's StratifiedKFold (classification) and KFold (regression), shuffled by PCG instead of numpy. All features are kept in every fold (q2's DictVectorizer drops features absent from a fold's training samples).

  • Float32: values are rounded to single precision before growing and predicting, as scikit-learn does; values that differ only beyond that (a relative 6e-8) are ties.

  • Not ported: q2's recursive feature elimination (but feature_volatility() has it) (optimize_feature_selection) and randomized parameter search, and scikit-learn's bootstrap = FALSE, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease, min_weight_fraction_leaf, ccp_alpha, monotonic_cst and missing values (NA in counts is an error).

Machine learning

Log-ratio transforms (clr, rclr, alr, ilr, PhILR) serve interpretation and compositional geometry; don't expect them to improve prediction. With random forests predicting 65 metadata variables in four datasets, Yerke et al. (2024) found that alr, clr and ilr (PhILR) "performed generally slightly worse or only as well as compositionally naïve transformations", and relative abundances did best, by a small margin. Compare with norm = 'percent' (see normalize()) before choosing a log-ratio predictor table.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

Pseudocount

The pseudocount parameter is only relevant when norm = 'clr' or norm = 'log'.

Zeros are undefined in the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation and in the log of proportions. If norm is 'clr' or 'log', pseudocount is NULL (the default), and zeros are detected, the function uses half the minimum non-zero value (min(x[x>0]) / 2) and issues a warning.

To suppress the warning, provide an explicit value (e.g., 1), or replace the zeros first with replace_zeros(), whose result needs no pseudocount.

Why this matters: The choice of pseudocount is not neutral; it acts as a weighting factor that can significantly distort downstream results, especially for sparse datasets. See Gloor et al. (2017) and Kaul et al. (2017) for open-access discussions on the mathematical implications, or Costea et al. (2014) for the impact on community clustering.

See aitchison for references.

See also

predict.ecodive_random_forest(), plot.ecodive_random_forest(), plsda(), lda()

Examples

    # Which body site? 20 samples from 4 sites, 5-fold cross-validation.
    counts <- ex_counts[rep(1:4, each = 5), ] + outer(1:20, 1:6) %% 7
    site   <- rep(rownames(ex_counts), each = 5)
    fit    <- random_forest(counts, site, n_trees = 50, cpus = 1)
    fit
#> # Random forest classification: 20 samples x 6 features
#> # 50 trees; max_features = 2, min_samples_leaf = 1, criterion = gini
#> # Classes: Gums, Nose, Saliva, Stool
#> # 5-fold CV accuracy: 1.00 (folds 1.00 +/- 0; baseline 0.250, ratio 4.00)
#> # CV AUC: macro 1.00, micro 1.00
#> # Out-of-bag accuracy: 1.00
#> # Top 6 features by impurity importance:
#>            feature impurity
#>      Streptococcus   0.3300
#>        Haemophilus   0.1920
#>  Propionibacterium   0.1510
#>     Staphylococcus   0.1480
#>        Bacteroides   0.1090
#>    Corynebacterium   0.0702

    # Predict new samples.
    predict(fit, ex_counts, cpus = 1)
#> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool 
#> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool 
#> Levels: Gums Nose Saliva Stool
